idiom_name: Thread::Mutex#synchronize (or Monitor for a reentrant lock object)
implementation_notes: Ruby's standard library provides the lock object and the scoped idiom: Thread::Mutex#synchronize acquires, runs the block and releases on every exit path including exceptions, Mutex#try_lock covers fail-fast acquisition, and Monitor - documented exactly as the lock object to use when you want mutual exclusion for blocks - adds reentrancy and condition variables (mon_synchronize, wait/signal). A class therefore holds a Mutex or Monitor and either publishes it or exposes synchronize-wrapped methods; with MRI's GVL the interpreter schedules threads cooperatively, so a mutex is still required for read-modify-write sequences, and JRuby/TruffleRuby run threads truly in parallel.
pitfalls: Mutex#synchronize is not reentrant: calling another synchronizing method of the same object from inside the block raises a deadlock error - use Monitor#mon_synchronize or unlocked private helpers.
The GVL prevents some interleaving but not races around blocking I/O, and it does not exist in every Ruby implementation; a published Mutex is the portable answer.

Publishing the lock means callers can hold it while calling the object's public methods, which deadlocks against those methods' own synchronize calls: document that only unlocked helpers may be used by a lock holder.
Monitor#synchronize and Mutex#synchronize are different objects with different reentrancy; mixing both for one piece of state creates two exclusion domains.
